verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 13.8 in the 34-verse numbering of chapter 13 used by Gita Press and by Mahadeva Sastri (Shankara), Govindacharya (Ramanuja), Vireswarananda (Sridhara) and Sivananda; 13.9 where Arjuna's opening question is counted as verse 1 (e.g. ISKCON). Text identical.
attribution_note: Krishna to Arjuna, part of the list of qualities that count as 'knowledge' (13.7-11 / 13.8-12).
translation_note: Accurate. 'duhkha-dosha-anudarshanam' can be read either as seeing the defect in birth, death, old age, disease and pain (five items) or as seeing pain itself as the defect in the first four; Shankara allows both.
context: Krishna has just called the body the 'field' and the self its 'knower', and now lists about twenty traits that together he calls knowledge: humility, patience, purity, steadiness and so on. This verse adds dispassion toward sense pleasures, freedom from ego, and repeated reflection on what birth, death, old age and illness involve. The list ends by calling everything opposite to it ignorance, and Krishna then turns to what is to be known.

key_terms.sense: dispassion toward the objects of the senses, the things that give pleasure
absence of ego; not identifying with the body or claiming as 'mine' what is not one's own (Ramanuja)
seeing again and again, reflecting on, the flaw or defect in something
birth, death, old age and disease: the unavoidable conditions of having a body

core_teaching: Knowledge shows itself as a changed relationship to pleasure and to the self-image: a person who honestly reflects on what embodied life involves loses the compulsive pull of sense pleasures and turns inward. The reflection is a means to dispassion, not an end in itself.

commentaries.gist: Dispassion toward pleasures seen and unseen. Reflect on the evil in birth, death, old age (decline, contempt), sickness and pain; or: these are miseries because they cause pain. This breeds indifference to bodily pleasure and turns the senses inward.

Dispassion is distaste for what is not the self, seeing its defects; non-egoism is not taking the body for the self or claiming what is not 'mine'. Reflection: while embodied, birth, death, ageing and disease are unavoidable.
Takes 7-11 as one list of means to knowing the pure self; 'seeing' means repeatedly pondering the misery and evil bound up with birth, death, old age and sickness.

The wise person's senses no longer run after objects and he does not even like to talk about them; egoism is the thought 'I am superior to all'; he never forgets the troubles of birth, ageing and sickness.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a reality check: remembering that bodies age and fall ill loosens the grip of status and constant gratification and makes room for what lasts. Sivananda defines the ego to be dropped very concretely, as the feeling 'I am better than everyone'.
misreadings: Not a call to despise the body or to dwell morbidly on death and disease.
Not saying pleasure is evil; the point is freedom from its compulsive pull.
Not a claim that life is only suffering; Shankara says birth and the rest are painful because they cause pain, not in their own nature.
cautions: Names death, old age and disease directly; for someone newly diagnosed, caring for a dying parent, or freshly bereaved, 'reflect on the defect of illness' can feel cold.
For readers prone to health anxiety or depressive rumination, contemplating disease and death may amplify distress; frame as perspective, not as an exercise to dwell on.
speaks_to: Restlessness from chasing pleasure, novelty or status and still feeling empty
Ego bruises and the need to look important
Midlife or ageing reflections: what actually matters when the body changes
Wanting to simplify and live with fewer cravings
not_for: Fresh grief or a new serious diagnosis
Health anxiety or obsessive fears about illness
Someone already anhedonic or depressed for whom 'turn away from pleasure' reads as confirmation

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 13.24 in the 34-verse numbering of chapter 13 used by Gita Press and by Mahadeva Sastri (Shankara), Govindacharya (Ramanuja), Vireswarananda (Sridhara) and Sivananda; 13.25 where Arjuna's opening question is counted as verse 1 (e.g. ISKCON). Text identical.
translation_note: Accurate. 'sāṅkhyena yogena' is usually read as the discipline of discriminating knowledge; Sridhara alone splits it into Sankhya and eight-limbed yoga as separate means. Our line's 'thinking it through' is a fair plain-English gloss.
context: Krishna has explained that the self is a witness distinct from nature (prakriti) and that whoever understands this is not reborn. Here he names the different routes by which people come to see that self. The next verse adds a further group who simply hear the teaching from others and practise it with faith.

key_terms.sense: meditation; Shankara describes it as an unbroken flow of attention, like oil poured from a vessel
the discipline of discrimination: knowing oneself as the witness, distinct from the three gunas
action done as an offering, which purifies the mind and so leads to knowledge
the self seen by means of the (purified) mind

core_teaching: There is more than one route to the same inner realisation: meditation, discriminating knowledge, and selfless action. Commentators read these as suited to different temperaments and stages, not as rival truths.

commentaries.gist: Meditation withdraws the senses into the mind and the mind into inner awareness, an unbroken flow 'like oil'. Sankhya is reflecting 'the gunas act; I am their witness'. Action done for the Lord counts as yoga by purifying the mind.

The perfected see the self through meditation; less advanced ones ready the mind through the path of knowledge; those unfit for it, those preferring an easier road, and public figures setting an example follow karma-yoga, which carries knowledge within it.

These are alternative routes to the same discriminating knowledge (he adds Patanjali's eight-limbed yoga as a fourth). They can be practised in sequence, but are listed separately because people differ in which they take up.
Many paths suit different temperaments: meditation, analytical inquiry that identifies with the silent witness, and karma-yoga that offers action and its fruit to the Lord.

practical_reading: Modern teachers use it to reassure people who 'can't meditate': some find depth in stillness, some in study and reflection, some in honest work done for others. Pick the route that fits your nature and do it wholeheartedly.
misreadings: Not 'any path is fine, so no discipline is needed'; each route is a demanding practice.
Not a ranking that dismisses action; Ramanuja treats karma-yoga as a complete means.
cautions: Doctrinal and comparatively abstract; better for a 'why/steady' day than for acute distress.
speaks_to: Feeling like a failure at meditation
Wondering whether one's spiritual practice is 'the right one'
Active, practical people who think spirituality isn't for them
Couples or families with different styles of practice
not_for: Acute crisis where the reader needs comfort rather than a map of paths
research_note: Our_note says Shankara grades the three paths as best, middling and others. In Mahadeva Sastri's translation the grading (highest, middling, lowest class of aspirants) appears in footnotes marked 'A.', i.e. Anandagiri's sub-commentary, not in Shankara's own text. Suggest attributing the grading to Anandagiri or dropping it.

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 13.25 in the 34-verse numbering of chapter 13 used by Gita Press and by Mahadeva Sastri (Shankara), Govindacharya (Ramanuja), Vireswarananda (Sridhara) and Sivananda; 13.26 where Arjuna's opening question is counted as verse 1 (e.g. ISKCON). Text identical.
translation_note: Accurate. 'mṛtyum' is read by Shankara as the cycle of birth and death (samsara), not physical death.
context: Right after naming meditation, discriminating knowledge and selfless action as routes to seeing the self, Krishna adds a fourth group: people who cannot follow any of those but hear the truth from teachers and worship or reflect with faith. Then he goes on to explain that everything that is born arises from the union of field and knower.

key_terms.sense: not knowing (these methods), unable to discern for themselves
having heard from others, from teachers
they worship, contemplate, keep returning to what they heard
those for whom listening is the supreme support
they cross beyond death, i.e. beyond the round of birth and death

core_teaching: Even someone with no capacity for subtle philosophy or demanding practice is not shut out: hearing the truth from trustworthy teachers and living by it with faith also carries a person across. The door is open to the ordinary seeker.

commentaries.gist: Some cannot know the self by these means; they learn from teachers and contemplate the teaching with full faith, relying wholly on others' instruction. Even they cross beyond death; how much more those who can weigh evidence themselves.

Those not yet able for the paths hear sages who have seen the truth; even those who can only believe what they hear are purged of sin and gradually take up karma-yoga. 'Also' marks these degrees of capacity.

A means of release for the least equipped: not knowing how to realise the self by knowledge or yoga, they meditate on what they hear from teachers and, devoted with faith to that hearing, slowly pass beyond transmigratory existence.

Calls this the yoga of worship: some listen with unshakable faith to their teachers, others study books by realised sages and live by them; they too overcome death, since there are paths to suit every temperament.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to honour the listener: you don't have to be a scholar or an adept; attending to good teaching, trusting it and returning to it daily is itself a path. It is a warm verse for beginners and for those who learn by ear.
misreadings: Not 'blind belief is enough'; Ramanuja and Sridhara describe listening as the start of gradual purification and practice.
'Crossing death' is not a promise that oneself or a loved one will be spared physical death.
cautions: Mentions death; in grief, 'they cross beyond death' may be heard as a promise about a loved one's fate, which the verse does not make.
speaks_to: Feeling not clever, educated or disciplined enough for spiritual life
Beginners and people who learn by listening (satsang, katha, podcasts)
Older readers who come to scripture late
Self-doubt about one's spiritual worth
not_for: Someone harmed by a manipulative teacher or group, for whom 'rely on what others tell you' could reopen that wound

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 13.27 in the 34-verse numbering of chapter 13 used by Gita Press and by Mahadeva Sastri (Shankara), Govindacharya (Ramanuja), Vireswarananda (Sridhara) and Sivananda; 13.28 where Arjuna's opening question is counted as verse 1 (e.g. ISKCON). Text identical.
translation_note: Accurate to Shankara's reading. Ramanuja reads 'parameshvara' here as the individual self, the ruler of its own body and senses, rather than God; worth knowing if a plan leans on 'the Supreme Lord'.
context: Krishna has just said that everything that comes into being arises from the joining of the field (body, nature) and its knower. He now says that the one who sees the same imperishable reality in all perishing beings is the one who truly sees. The next verse says such a person no longer harms the self by the self.

key_terms.sense: equally, the same, without distinction
the supreme Lord (Shankara); for Ramanuja, the self as ruler of body, senses and mind
the undying within things that die
whoever sees this, truly sees

core_teaching: True seeing is recognising one unchanging reality present equally in every living being, which does not perish when bodies perish. Everything else is a partial or distorted view.

commentaries.gist: The Supreme Lord dwells without difference in all beings, from Brahma to the unmoving, imperishable while they perish. All see, but wrongly, like a diseased eye seeing several moons; only one who sees the one undivided self truly sees.

'Supreme lord' here is the self, ruler of the body, senses and mind it dwells in. Seeing it as the same knower in every body, apart from divine, human or other forms, and undecaying while bodies decay, is true seeing.

Having described the bondage that comes from lack of discrimination, Krishna gives its cure: seeing the Supreme Lord present equally, as pure existence, in all moving and unmoving beings, and not perishing when they perish. Only that person sees rightly.
Heat is the same in different fires, gold in different ornaments, light from many lamps; so the one Lord in all beings, who is not destroyed when they are.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to how we treat people: the same worth lives in a beggar and a king, a rival and a friend. It is also used, gently and later in mourning, to say that what was most real in a person is not destroyed with the body.
misreadings: Not a denial that loss is real or that bodies and lives matter.
Not a reason to be indifferent to suffering because 'the self is untouched'.
cautions: Mentions perishing; in fresh grief 'the undying within the dying' can sound like 'nothing was really lost'. Use only once the reader is ready for consolation of this kind.
speaks_to: Prejudice, contempt or feeling superior to others
Loneliness and a sense of separateness
Caregivers and hospice workers looking for meaning
Grief some time after a loss, when the reader seeks what endures
not_for: The first days of a bereavement
Someone angry at platitudes about the soul

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 13.28 in the 34-verse numbering of chapter 13 used by Gita Press and by Mahadeva Sastri (Shankara), Govindacharya (Ramanuja), Vireswarananda (Sridhara) and Sivananda; 13.29 where Arjuna's opening question is counted as verse 1 (e.g. ISKCON). Text identical.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Does not injure the self by the self' is literal; Shankara and Sridhara read it as not obscuring or 'killing' one's true self through ignorance.
context: Following the statement that true seeing finds the same undying reality in all beings, Krishna gives its result: the one who sees this does not harm the self by the self and reaches the highest goal. He goes on to say that it is nature that acts, while the self is not the doer.

key_terms.sense: the Lord (or, for Ramanuja, the self) present equally everywhere
does not injure or destroy the self by the self
the highest goal, liberation

core_teaching: Seeing the same reality in all beings ends the way we wound ourselves: mistaking ourselves for the body and its fortunes. That clear sight is what leads to freedom.

commentaries.gist: No one literally destroys himself; but the ignorant ignore the self, take the body for it and lose body after body, so they are 'slayers of the self'. One who sees the Lord everywhere is not, and is liberated.

'Lord' is the soul, ruler and support of every body; seeing it as the same conscious knower in all bodies, one does not harm it by wrong thinking, saves it from samsara, and reaches the highest goal, seeing the self.

Seeing the Lord equally present everywhere, one does not through ignorance deny one's own nature of existence, awareness and bliss, and so gains liberation; one who takes the body for the self kills the self along with the body.
The ignorant 'destroy the Self' by identifying with the body and the mind's changes and failing to see the one Self in all; the liberated sage sees it everywhere.

practical_reading: Teachers read it as: much of our suffering is self-inflicted through a narrow, body-bound view of who we are, and widening that view to see the same life in others also eases how we treat ourselves.
misreadings: Not about self-harm in the clinical sense; 'killing the self' is a metaphor for ignorance of one's nature.
Not saying the body or physical health doesn't matter.
cautions: The traditional language of 'self-slayers' (and Sridhara's citation of the Isha Upanishad line about such people going to sunless worlds) must never be used with a reader who mentions self-harm or suicidal thoughts; route those to real help instead.
Avoid phrasing that implies a struggling reader is 'hurting themselves' by not seeing correctly.
speaks_to: Harsh self-criticism and inner conflict
Feeling cut off from others
Wanting a wider, kinder sense of self
not_for: Any reader expressing self-harm or suicidal thoughts
Someone already blaming themselves for their pain

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 13.32 in the 34-verse numbering of chapter 13 used by Gita Press and by Mahadeva Sastri (Shankara), Govindacharya (Ramanuja), Vireswarananda (Sridhara) and Sivananda; 13.33 where Arjuna's opening question is counted as verse 1 (e.g. ISKCON). Text identical.
translation_note: Accurate. 'ākāśa' is space or ether rather than the visible sky; 'sky' works as an image. 'dehe' is singular but, as Sridhara's gloss ('in every body, superior, middling or inferior') shows, means every body.
context: Krishna has said that the supreme self, though dwelling in the body, neither acts nor is tainted. This verse gives the first of two images: space pervades everything yet nothing clings to it. The next verse adds the image of the one sun lighting the whole world.

key_terms.sense: all-pervading space
because of its subtlety
is not smeared, stained or affected

core_teaching: The self present in every body is not stained by what the body does or undergoes, just as space contains everything and is soiled by none of it.

commentaries.gist: As all-pervading space, being subtle, is never soiled, so the self present everywhere in the body is not soiled. (A footnote from Anandagiri adds that space pervades mire and the like without being affected.)

Space is in contact with everything yet, being subtle, takes on none of their properties; the self, very subtle, dwells in the bodies of gods, humans and others without being sullied by their peculiar qualities.
As space is present even in mud but, being subtle and untouched, is not muddied, so the self in a superior, middling or lowly body is not joined to that body's merits or defects.
Being subtler than the body, the self, like ether, pervades all yet is tainted by nothing; it is unattached and actionless, so virtue and vice cannot touch it.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to separate who you are from what has happened to you or around you: illness, ageing, social status or past events do not soil your deepest identity. It is also used against judging people by their bodies, caste or circumstances.
misreadings: Not a licence to act carelessly because 'my self is untouched'; the Gita elsewhere holds people responsible for their actions.
Not a denial that harm done to a person is real.
cautions: For survivors of abuse or assault, 'you are unstained' can be healing, but should never imply the harm did not matter or that they should simply rise above it.
speaks_to: Shame or feeling 'dirty' because of the past
Body image struggles, illness or disability affecting self-worth
Being judged by status, caste or background
Wanting an image of inner spaciousness for meditation
not_for: Someone using it to excuse their own harmful actions
A reader who needs their hurt acknowledged first
research_note: Our_note attributes to Shankara 'not touched by the body's actions and their fruits'; his comment on this verse (Mahadeva Sastri) says only that the self, like space, is not soiled; the point about actions belongs to the surrounding verses (13.31).

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 14.8 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda)
translation_note: Translation accurate. Our line adds 'too much' to sleep; the verse says only 'sleep' (nidra). Commentators treat it as one of tamas's binding channels, not sleep as such, so the gloss is defensible but interpretive.
context: Krishna is describing how each of the three gunas binds the embodied self: sattva through attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas through attachment to action, and here tamas through heedlessness, laziness and sleep. The next verses summarise and then give the signs by which each guna can be recognised.

key_terms.sense: the guna of darkness, inertia and dullness
born of ignorance (Ramanuja: of mistaken knowledge)
heedlessness, inattention to what should be done
laziness, reluctance to begin anything
sleep; Sridhara: the mind sinking into dullness

core_teaching: Dullness clouds judgement and holds a person down through inattention, inertia and sinking into sleep. Naming it is the first step to rising out of it.

commentaries.gist: Very brief: tamas, the third guna, is born of unwisdom and causes delusion, that is, non-discrimination, in all embodied beings, binding them through heedlessness, indolence and sloth.

Ignorance is the reverse of right perception, seeing a thing as other than it is. Heedlessness is attention drifting from the task at hand; sloth is inability to engage in work; sleep is the senses, then the mind, shutting down.
Tamas comes from nature's concealing power and so confounds every embodied being. Inadvertence is negligence, laziness is lack of effort, and sleep is the mind shutting down through fatigue.
Tamas tends to lethargy and foolish action; the tamasic person is driven by the body's wants, acting under pressure rather than guided by reason or judgement.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a self-check on drift: scrolling, putting things off, sleeping to escape. The remedy suggested is small, steady attention and action rather than self-blame.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of rest or sleep; nidra here is sleep used as escape or dullness.
Not a moral label for people who are ill, exhausted or depressed.
cautions: Symptoms of depression, burnout, chronic illness, medication side effects and new-parent exhaustion overlap with 'laziness and sleep'; never frame these as tamas or a character flaw.
Sivananda's commentary is harsh in tone; do not echo that harshness to a struggling reader.
speaks_to: Procrastination and drifting days
Using sleep, screens or substances to avoid life
Wanting to understand one's own sluggish patterns without shame
not_for: Someone in depression or burnout
Chronic fatigue or illness
Sleep-deprived new parents

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 14.12 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda)
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Krishna gives the signs by which a person can tell which guna is dominant: when clarity and knowledge shine through the senses, sattva has grown (14.11); this verse gives the signs of rajas; the next gives those of tamas. He goes on to say what each leads to at death and as fruit.

key_terms.sense: greed; Shankara: wanting others' goods; Ramanuja: unwillingness to give up one's own; Sridhara: desire that grows as wealth grows
constant activity, being always busy
undertaking (new) projects and ventures
no rest; the mind never settling
craving, thirst for whatever one sees

core_teaching: Greed, compulsive busyness, endless new ventures, inner restlessness and craving are the signs that rajas has taken over. They are diagnostic signs to notice, not a verdict on action itself.

commentaries.gist: Greed is wanting to take others' property; activity is action in general; unrest is giving vent to joy, attachment and the like; desire is thirst for all things in general. These are the marks of rajas predominating.

Greed is close-fistedness with one's own money; activity is busyness without definite purpose; undertaking is fruit-seeking work; disquiet is restlessness of the senses; craving is for sense-objects. Seeing these, infer that rajas is ascendant.

Greed is desire for wealth that keeps growing however much is gained; undertakings are efforts like building houses; restlessness is the constant 'after this I'll do that'; desire is wanting whatever one sees, good or bad.
Greed includes wanting more wealth though one has enough; restlessness is 'I'll do this, then that, then a third': desire, will and action never end.

practical_reading: A close fit for modern burnout: the to-do list that never ends, starting new projects before finishing old ones, and wanting more as soon as one gets something. Teachers suggest noticing these signs early and pausing before acting on them.
misreadings: Not a condemnation of work or ambition; the Gita elsewhere commands action.
Not saying all new projects are bad; the issue is compulsion and restlessness.
cautions: Generally safe. Avoid making a reader feel judged for having to work long hours out of necessity.
speaks_to: Burnout, overwork, hustle culture
Shopping, scrolling or acquiring compulsively
A mind that won't switch off at night
Entrepreneurs juggling too many ventures
not_for: Someone in poverty or financial distress for whom 'greed' framing about earning would be unfair

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 14.13 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda)
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Third in a set of three verses giving recognisable signs of each guna: sattva (14.11), rajas (14.12) and here tamas. Krishna then describes where a person goes at death depending on which guna prevails.

key_terms.sense: darkness, loss of discernment
inertia, no effort or initiative
heedlessness, losing sight of what needs doing
delusion, confused or mistaken understanding

core_teaching: When tamas grows, the mind loses clarity, effort dries up, attention slips and judgement becomes confused. Recognising these signs lets a person see what state they are in.

commentaries.gist: Darkness is absence of discrimination; inertness, its result, is extreme inactivity; heedlessness and error are also effects of that darkness. These mark tamas predominating.

Obscurity is absence of understanding; inertness is disinclination to work; heedlessness is attention turned toward wrongdoing; error is the intellect's tendency to see things distorted. Where these are rife, infer tamas is ascendant.
Darkness is lack of discrimination, inactivity is absence of effort, inadvertence is not remembering one's duty, and delusion is a mistaken resolve. By these signs know tamas has increased.
When tamas grows there is darkness, a wish to do nothing, forgetting one's duties and confusion; he calls tamas a great stumbling block to spiritual progress.

practical_reading: Used as a mirror for foggy, stuck periods: noticing 'I can't see clearly, I'm not starting anything, I keep missing things' is itself the first bit of clarity. Teachers pair it with small, concrete steps.
misreadings: Not a diagnosis of anyone's character.
Not identical to depression; overlapping symptoms need care, not moral judgement.
cautions: The signs (fog, inertia, confusion) closely resemble clinical depression, grief and burnout; never imply the reader is 'tamasic' or to blame.
Sivananda's commentary says tamas must be destroyed at all costs; avoid that tone with distressed readers.
speaks_to: Feeling stuck, foggy or directionless
Procrastination and missed responsibilities
Wanting language to observe one's own low states
not_for: Someone in depression, grief or burnout
A reader who already feels like a failure

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 14.22 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda)
attribution_note: Krishna answering Arjuna's three questions in 14.21 (signs, conduct, and means of going beyond the gunas).
translation_note: Accurate. Data glitch: our Sanskrit field runs the speaker tag into the verse with no break ('श्री भगवानुवाचप्रकाशं'). Our line turns a description into an instruction ('Don't hate your moods'), which is fine for the app but note that the verse describes the one beyond the gunas.
context: Arjuna has asked how to recognise someone who has gone beyond the three gunas, how such a person behaves, and how they get there. Krishna's answer runs through 14.26; this first verse gives an inner sign. Sridhara notes Arjuna had asked a similar question about the person of steady wisdom in chapter 2.

key_terms.sense: clarity, activity and delusion: the effects of sattva, rajas and tamas
does not resent them when they arise
does not long for them when they have gone

core_teaching: One who has gone beyond the gunas neither resents clarity, restlessness or dullness when they arise, nor craves them when they pass. The mark is an inner freedom from aversion and longing toward one's own changing states.

commentaries.gist: The unknowing resent these states: 'tamas deludes me', 'rajas pulls me from my true nature', 'even sattva binds me to happiness'. The one beyond the gunas neither resents nor longs for them; only he can perceive this mark.

Lucidity, activity and folly are the effects of the three gunas; the sign of one beyond them is not hating them when they arise toward unwanted things and not longing for them when they are absent toward wanted things.

Though the steady sage was described in chapter 2, Arjuna wants detail, so six verses follow. This one gives a sign known only to oneself: not hating the gunas' effects as they arise, nor wanting them when they cease.
Answers Arjuna's first question; when sattva shines the sage is not proud of his learning, and when called to act for the world he acts without aversion.

practical_reading: Modern teachers read it as a way to relate to moods: low days and high days both come and go, and fighting the low or clinging to the high adds a second layer of suffering. Notice the state without hating it or chasing it.
misreadings: Not 'feel nothing' or suppress emotion.
Not a reason to ignore persistent low mood that needs care.
cautions: Gentle and broadly safe; still, a reader in clinical depression should not hear 'just don't mind it'.
speaks_to: Mood swings and frustration with one's own states
Meditators fighting distraction or dullness
Chasing peak experiences and feeling flat afterwards
Self-judgement about 'bad days'
not_for: Someone in acute crisis needing practical help rather than acceptance language

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 14.23 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda)
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Part of Krishna's answer (14.22-26) to Arjuna's question about the person beyond the gunas. After the inner sign in 14.22, this verse begins describing how such a person conducts himself. It continues with equanimity in pleasure and pain, praise and blame.

key_terms.sense: sitting like one who takes no side, a neutral onlooker
is not shaken, not moved from himself
'it is the gunas that are acting'
does not waver

core_teaching: The one beyond the gunas stays like a neutral witness, not pushed around by the play of moods and circumstances, knowing that these are nature's movements and not the self.

commentaries.gist: Like a neutral who takes no side, the self-knowing renunciate does not swerve from discrimination; thinking 'the gunas, turned into body, senses and objects, act on one another', he stays unshaken in his own nature.

Delighting in seeing the self, he is indifferent to all else; unagitated by the desires and aversions the gunas produce, he reflects that it is their nature to display themselves, keeps quiet, and does not act at their prompting.

Begins the signs others can see, answering 'how does he behave?': he rests like a witness, not shaken from his nature by pleasure and pain, knowing 'I have no connection with these', steady and unwavering.
He is like a spectator at a match or a play, or the sky unmoved when the wind blows, free of likes and dislikes as the gunas come and go.

practical_reading: Teachers connect it to witness practice in meditation and daily life: stepping back half a pace from a surge of anger or anxiety and saying 'this is a state passing through' before reacting.
misreadings: Not emotional numbness or not caring about people.
Not passivity in the face of wrong; Arjuna is still asked to act.

commentaries.gist: Tejas means energy, not bright skin. Forgiveness is being unaffected when beaten or reviled, unlike absence of anger, which suppresses it once arisen. Fortitude lifts a drooping body and senses. Pride is thinking oneself worthy of high honour.

commentaries.gist: 'Evil' action is desire-driven work that perpetuates samsara; he does not hate it. 'Good' is obligatory work; he is not attached to it as a means to liberation. Permeated by discriminating sattva, he gains wisdom and his doubts are cut.

Having renounced attachment, fruit and agency, full of sattva and doubt-free, he is neither troubled by acts with unwanted results nor attached to those yielding heaven, children or cattle, since 'mine' is gone and every end but Brahman given up.

He does not hate painful work, like a dawn bath in winter, nor relish pleasant work, like a noon bath in summer; one who endures humiliation and forgoes heaven's joys reasons that such passing pleasures and pains hardly matter.
All actions are equally welcome to him; he is neither elated by pleasant work nor put off by disagreeable work.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to the parts of a job or role we love and hate: do the tedious paperwork without sulking, and the glamorous work without getting possessive. Sridhara's cold-bath example makes it concrete.
misreadings: Not that one should have no preferences at all, or must accept harmful work.
Not indifference to quality; it is about not being ruled by liking and disliking.
cautions: Broadly safe.
speaks_to: Resenting boring or unpleasant parts of work or caregiving
Getting possessive over the 'fun' tasks
Wanting steadier motivation
not_for: Someone in genuinely harmful or degrading work who needs to change it

one who gives up the fruit of action
a true renouncer

core_teaching: As long as we live in a body we cannot stop acting, so the real renunciation is giving up our claim on the results, not giving up action.

commentaries.gist: 'Body-wearer' means one who identifies with the body; such a person cannot give up action completely, so doing obligatory work while giving up only the fruit, he is called an abandoner by courtesy. Only the knower can abandon all action.

One in a body cannot give up work entirely, since getting food and drink is unavoidable; so the daily rites remain, and one who gives up their fruit, which implies giving up agency and attachment too, is the true renouncer.

Wouldn't renouncing all action be better for undistracted knowledge? No: one who identifies with the body cannot give it up entirely (3.5), so one who keeps acting while relinquishing the fruit is the real relinquisher.

practical_reading: A liberating verse for busy people: spirituality is not about escaping work but changing your relationship to its payoff. You can be fully engaged and inwardly free.
misreadings: Not that the renunciate life is worthless; Shankara keeps full renunciation for the realised.
Not 'don't care about results' as an excuse for sloppy work.
cautions: Broadly safe.
speaks_to: Householders who feel spiritual life requires leaving the world
Burnout from outcome-anxiety
Wanting to work without being consumed by results

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.16 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda)
translation_note: Translation is defensible. 'ātmānaṃ kevalam' can mean 'oneself alone' (Ramanuja) or 'the pure, unconditioned self' (Shankara, Sridhara), so for Shankara the error is attributing agency to the actionless self. Our line's 'alone made it fail' is a modern extension to blame and guilt, reasonable but interpretive.
context: Krishna has listed five factors behind every action of body, speech or mind: the body as base, the doer, the instruments, the various efforts, and providence (daiva) (18.13-15). key_terms.sense: the self alone (or the pure self) as the doer
because the understanding is untrained, unrefined
he does not see
of mistaken or perverse understanding

core_teaching: Every action arises from several factors together. Seeing oneself as the sole author of what happens, for good or ill, is a failure of understanding.

commentaries.gist: Every act is done by the five causes; the ignorant, untrained by Vedanta, teacher or reasoning, identify with them and see the pure Self as agent. Seeing, they do not see, like a passenger who thinks he is running.

The individual self is an agent, but only with the Supreme Self's sanction; whoever thinks his own self acts with full independence has a warped understanding and does not see the other factors that make up his agency.

Since these five cause all action, whoever, with an understanding unrefined by scripture and teacher, regards the Self, free of adjuncts and unattached, as the agent is foolish and does not see truly.
The Self is always actionless, the silent witness of activity; the egoistic person thinks himself the real agent and so is bound by actions.

practical_reading: Teachers use it two ways: against pride ('I did this all myself') and against crushing guilt ('it was all my fault'). Many factors, including circumstance and grace, shape every outcome.
misreadings: Not a way to dodge responsibility; you are still one of the five causes.
Not 'nothing is my doing'; Ramanuja insists the self is a real agent.
Do not chain it to 18.17 ('even if he kills') without careful framing.
cautions: Can ease survivor's guilt or self-blame after a loss, but must not be used to dismiss the feeling or to excuse real wrongdoing.
The next verse (18.17) about killing is easily misread; keep readings on this verse.
speaks_to: Self-blame after a failure or loss
Pride in sole credit for success
Team settings where blame is being assigned
Perfectionists who feel everything rests on them
not_for: Someone avoiding accountability for harm they caused
A reader who needs their guilt heard before it is reframed

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.20 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda)
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Krishna has said that knowledge, action and the doer each come in three kinds according to the gunas (18.19). This verse gives sattvic knowledge: seeing one undivided reality in all beings. Rajasic knowledge sees only separate entities (18.21), and tamasic knowledge clings to one small thing as if it were everything (18.22).

key_terms.sense: one imperishable reality
undivided in the divided
sees, perceives
knowledge of the clear, balanced kind

core_teaching: The clearest kind of knowledge sees a single, unchanging reality running through all beings, undivided even though they appear separate.

commentaries.gist: Knowledge that sees one immutable Self in all beings, from unmanifest matter to unmoving things, undivided across bodies as space is, is direct right perception of the non-dual Self and is sattvic. Dualistic systems are rajasic or tamasic.

Beings are divided as brahmana, kshatriya, student, householder and so on, or as fair or tall; seeing in them one self, alike as consciousness, unchanging amid changing bodies, with no stake in the act's fruit, is sattvic knowledge.
The knowledge that sees, in all beings from Brahma to the unmoving, distinct from one another, the one undivided, imperishable, changeless substance, the Supreme Self, is sattvic.
Pure knowledge sees no difference in what is perceived: one imperishable essence behind seeming diversity, unity in diversity, all things rooted in the One.

practical_reading: Teachers use it against tribalism and contempt: the same life looks out of every face, whatever the label of caste, class, religion or nation. It is also a meditation on unity.
misreadings: Not a denial that people differ or that differences matter in practical life.
Not a license to ignore injustice because 'all is one'.
cautions: Broadly safe.
speaks_to: Prejudice and polarisation
Feeling isolated or separate
Conflict with people unlike oneself
Interfaith or intercultural settings
not_for: No strong contraindications

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.23 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda)
translation_note: Accurate. Our line renders 'niyatam' as 'steady'; it means obligatory or regulated (for Ramanuja, suited to one's station).
context: After the three kinds of knowledge, Krishna turns to the three kinds of action. This is sattvic action; rajasic action (18.24) is driven by desire and ego and done with great strain, tamasic action (18.25) is begun blindly. The three kinds of doer follow.

key_terms.sense: obligatory, regulated, one's proper duty
free of attachment
done without being driven by liking or aversion
by one who does not crave the result

core_teaching: Good action is one's proper work done without clinging, without being pushed by likes and dislikes, and without craving its reward.

commentaries.gist: Brief gloss: 'ordained' means obligatory (nitya) action; sattvic action is not done under the impulse of love or hatred, and is done by one not desiring its fruit.

Duty is what is prescribed for one's varna and stage of life; done free of attachment such as the sense of agency, of love of fame and hatred of infamy (that is, without vanity), and of desire for fruit.
An action prescribed as a regular rite, done without hankering, not out of love for one's son or hatred toward an enemy, by a disinterested agent, is sattvic.
Such pure action is done wholeheartedly, offered to the Lord without caring for reward, and the doer experiences great joy.

practical_reading: A test for one's own work: am I doing this because it's right, or because I like it, hate someone, want praise or fear blame? Ramanuja's 'not for fame, not from fear of disgrace' is especially sharp.
misreadings: Not 'feel nothing while working'; it is about motive, not emotion.
Not a defence of duties that cause harm.
cautions: Broadly safe.
speaks_to: Workplace motives: reputation, rivalry, approval
Wanting cleaner, less ego-driven work
Parents and caregivers
not_for: No strong contraindications

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.24 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda)
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Second of three kinds of action (18.23-25): after sattvic action done without attachment or craving, this is rajasic action, done for desired ends, with ego, and with great strain. Tamasic action follows.

key_terms.sense: by one who wants to fulfil desires, seeks results
with ego, with a sense of 'I am doing this'
with great strain and effort

core_teaching: Action driven by desire for results and by ego, carried out with exhausting strain, is the restless rajasic kind.

commentaries.gist: Done for pleasures as fruit, by the egotistic, at great cost of effort. 'Egotistic' contrasts with an ordinary humble Vedic devotee, not the self-realised, who could never seek fruit or toil so; even a sattvic doer has some ego.
Done aiming at fruit, with the self-love of being its performer, and with great strain; that is, done with the conceit 'what an enormous work this is, and I have done it'.
Done by one craving fruit, or with deep-rooted egotism such as 'who else is a Vedic scholar like me?', and with great strain: such action is rajasic.
The passionate person boasts of his actions in public and can never work without expecting reward; only a liberated sage is wholly free of egoism.

practical_reading: Teachers link it to hustle and martyrdom: work done to prove oneself, with the inner narrative 'I'm the only one carrying all this', tends to be exhausting and brittle.
misreadings: Not saying hard work is bad; strain driven by ego and craving is the issue.
Not judging people who must work very hard to survive.
cautions: Avoid implying that someone overworking out of financial necessity is egoistic.
speaks_to: Burnout and overwork
The 'only I can do this' feeling
Competitive, status-driven workplaces
not_for: Someone working multiple jobs out of necessity

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.25 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda)
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Third of three kinds of action (18.23-25): tamasic action is begun in confusion, without weighing its consequences, cost, harm or one's own ability. Krishna then describes the three kinds of doer (18.26-28).

key_terms.sense: what follows, the consequences
loss, of wealth or strength
harm to living beings
one's own capacity to carry it through
out of confusion, lack of discernment

core_teaching: Action begun blindly, without considering consequences, cost, harm to others or one's own capacity, is the darkest kind.

commentaries.gist: Undertaken from delusion without regard to consequence, to the loss of power and wealth it will cause, to injury to living beings, or to one's own ability to complete it: such action is tamasic.

Done heedless of the pain that follows, the money it costs and the hurt it causes creatures, boasting that one can finish it, and from ignorance that the Supreme Person is the real doer: such action is tamasic.
Begun from sheer delusion, without considering the good or evil that will follow, the expense, injury to others, or one's own strength: such action is tamasic.
The tamasic person acts blindly, never asking whether he has the capacity, what it will cost or what will result, and so harms others.

practical_reading: Works as a four-point checklist before a big decision: What follows from this? What will it cost? Who could be hurt? Can I actually carry it through?
misreadings: Not a call to over-deliberate or never take risks; it targets acting blindly.
cautions: Avoid shaming someone who made an impulsive decision during a crisis.
speaks_to: Impulsive decisions: debts, risky ventures, angry messages
Young people facing big choices
Teams launching projects without planning
not_for: Someone already paralysed by over-thinking

translation_note: Accurate.

eager for the results of action
greedy
disposed to harm others
swung between elation and dejection

core_teaching: The restless kind of doer is attached, hungry for results, greedy, willing to harm, impure in motive, and thrown between elation at success and dejection at failure.

commentaries.gist: Greedy means thirsting for others' property and not giving one's own to the worthy; cruel means harming others; impure lacks outer and inner purity; he rejoices at what he wants and grieves at the unwanted or at losing the wanted.

He hungers for fame, power and honour, expects the benefit, will not spend what the work requires, gets it done through cruelty to others, lacks the purity work needs, and is enslaved by joy and grief at outcomes.

Attached to children and the like, longing for results, covetous of others' property, inclined to violence, not observing prescribed cleanliness, and elated or dejected at gain or loss: such an agent is rajasic.
He strives wholeheartedly wherever he imagines worldly gain, keeps whatever he gains for himself and his family, rejoices at success and is overcome by grief at failure.

practical_reading: A mirror for result-driven work: if every win sends you soaring and every setback crushes you, and you cut corners or step on people to get results, rajas is running the show.
misreadings: Not saying that feeling happy or sad about outcomes is a sin; it describes being swung by them.
Not a label to pin on colleagues.
cautions: 'Swayed by sorrow' should not be applied to someone grieving a real loss.
speaks_to: Result-obsessed work culture
Emotional roller-coaster of targets and reviews
Leaders who push people too hard
not_for: Someone grieving
Someone already crushed by a failure who needs comfort

deceitful, hiding one's real capacity

Unqualified for scripture-prescribed work, unlettered, disinclined even to begin, fond of sorcery, bent on imposing on others, slack in work begun, always gloomy, and harbouring deep, long vengeance against others: such is the tamasic agent.

Wanting honest self-examination

translation_note: Accurate. 'Ayathāvat' is 'not as it truly is' or, for Sridhara, 'in a doubtful way'; our line's 'can't quite tell' captures this half-clarity well.
context: Krishna sorts the intellect (buddhi) by the gunas. The sattvic intellect knows when to act and when to withdraw, what to do and avoid, what to fear and not, what binds and what frees (18.30). This verse is the rajasic intellect; the tamasic one, which inverts right and wrong, follows (18.32).

what should and should not be done

an intellect coloured by restlessness

core_teaching: An intellect clouded by restlessness does not discern right and wrong, or what to do and avoid, clearly; it is not inverted, just unreliable and mixed.

commentaries.gist: Dharma is what scripture ordains and adharma what it forbids; the rajasic intellect understands these, and what should and should not be done, wrongly, that is, contrary to what all authorities have settled.
It does not rightly discern the two kinds of dharma (of active life and of withdrawal) and their opposites, nor what a person ought and ought not to do according to time, place and circumstance.
'Incorrectly' means in a way that leaves one in doubt; the rest he calls self-evident.
No English word fits dharma: it is what raises you toward the Self, adharma what hurls you into ignorance; the rajasic intellect confuses them.

misreadings: Not saying every moral uncertainty is a character flaw; Ramanuja notes right action depends on time, place and circumstance.
cautions: Broadly safe.

Decisions made in a rush or while angry
Grey-area dilemmas at work

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.32 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda)
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Third of three kinds of intellect (18.30-32): after the clear sattvic intellect and the unreliable rajasic one, this is the tamasic intellect, covered by darkness, which takes wrong for right and sees everything in reverse. The three kinds of resolve (dhriti) follow.

key_terms.sense: takes wrong to be right
covered by darkness
all things the wrong way round

core_teaching: When the intellect is covered by darkness it does not merely blur right and wrong but inverts them, seeing everything upside down.

commentaries.gist: Very brief: enveloped in darkness, it sees adharma as dharma and takes a wholly perverted view of all things to be known.
Wrapped in tamas, it perceives everything contrariwise: wrong as right, right as wrong, fact as figment, fancy as fact, the higher ideal as base and the base as higher.

An understanding that grasps things in an inverted way is tamasic. Of the mind's many functions, understanding, tenacity and happiness are singled out because they chiefly lead to right and wrong, fear and fearlessness.
It treats virtues as vices and regards what scripture calls good as wholly wrong, viewing everything in a perverted light.

practical_reading: A warning about rationalisation: the mind can build convincing cases for what is clearly harmful. Teachers suggest checking big moral conclusions against trusted people and principles.
misreadings: Not a tool for labelling those who disagree with you as 'tamasic'.
cautions: Easily weaponised in arguments; keep it as self-examination.
speaks_to: Noticing one's own rationalisations
Situations where harmful behaviour has been normalised
Recovering from manipulation or propaganda
not_for: Someone being gaslit who may already doubt their own perceptions

translation_note: Accurate.

the workings of mind, breath (life-force) and senses
through unwavering yoga, steady concentration

core_teaching: The best kind of resolve, sustained by steady concentration, holds mind, breath and senses on course without wavering.

commentaries.gist: Yoga here is samadhi, concentration; the firmness always joined to it holds the activities of thought, breath and senses back from rushing into ways opposed to scripture. (Anandagiri's footnote: firmness without such concentration cannot reliably restrain them.)

Yoga is meditation on the Lord, the means to release, pursued single-mindedly; the purpose that keeps mind, vitality and senses engaged in achieving it, discarding every fruit opposed to liberation, is sattvic.
The tenacity that is unswerving, thinking of nothing else, through concentration of mind, and by which one regulates the functions of mind, breaths and senses, is sattvic.
Firmness alone cannot restrain mind, life-force and senses; it must be joined with concentration, by which the senses are withdrawn into the mind.

practical_reading: Teachers connect it to the steadiness built by daily practice: breath, attention and habits held on course by a clear purpose, rather than by willpower spikes.
misreadings: Not suppression or rigid self-control for its own sake; Ramanuja frames it as staying engaged toward a meaningful goal.
cautions: Broadly safe.
speaks_to: Building a meditation or study habit
Staying focused amid distraction
Long projects requiring perseverance
not_for: No strong contraindications

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.34 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda)
translation_note: Accurate; 'Arjuna' and 'Partha' are both in the Sanskrit.

key_terms.sense: duty, pleasure and wealth: the three worldly aims of life
with attachment; or, as each occasion arises
craving the fruit

core_teaching: Determination that pursues duty, pleasure and wealth for their payoffs is the restless kind of resolve: strong, but transactional.

commentaries.gist: When a person is firmly convinced that dharma, pleasure and wealth must always be secured, and desires the fruit of whichever one occupies his attention at the moment, his firmness is rajasic.

Dharma, pleasure and wealth here stand for the powers of mind, life and senses directed toward them; the will that, from longing for fruit and attachment, keeps those energies aimed at these ends rather than liberation is rajasic.
The tenacity that holds primarily to duty, pleasure and wealth, never letting them go, and through attachment becomes desirous of their fruit, is rajasic.
The person of rajasic firmness clings passionately to the threefold aim of life, dharma, wealth and pleasure, and wants the rewards of his actions.

practical_reading: A mirror for ambitious people: drive can be admirable and still be transactional, including 'being good' for the rewards it brings. Teachers invite keeping the drive and loosening the bargain.
misreadings: Not saying duty, pleasure or wealth are wrong; they are legitimate aims, and the issue is grasping for fruit.
cautions: Broadly safe.
speaks_to: Career-driven ambition
Doing good for recognition or reward
Feeling empty despite achieving goals
not_for: No strong contraindications

commentaries.gist: The dull person prizes sensual gratification and never gives up indulgence; he regards sleep, fear, grief, depression and lust as things always to be resorted to. That firmness is tamasic.

Madam is the stupor that comes from enjoying objects; the unwise person does not check, and even abets, the mind and life-forces dragging him into sleep and fancies; fear, grief and despair stand for the things that cause them.

Numbing habits (oversleeping, substances, endless scrolling)
Recognising patterns in recovery, once stable
