Clinical depression or anxiety
Anyone in crisis

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.36 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda). Sridhara and some editions read 36b with 37 as one sentence describing sattvic happiness.
translation_note: Accurate. Sridhara (Vireswarananda) reads the second line together with 18.37 as the start of the description of sattvic happiness; Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara keeps it in 18.36 and glosses it there. Our translation is compatible with both.
context: Having sorted knowledge, action, doer, intellect and resolve, Krishna turns to happiness. He introduces three kinds and begins with the best: the joy one grows into through practice, which ends sorrow. The next verse says it is like poison at first and nectar at the end; rajasic happiness (18.38) is the reverse.

key_terms.sense: threefold happiness
one comes to delight in it through repeated practice
reaches the end of sorrow

core_teaching: There is a happiness that does not arrive in a rush but grows through steady practice and familiarity, and it brings sorrow to an end.

commentaries.gist: Brief gloss: 'hear' means pay steady attention; 'practice' means familiarity and repetition; 'the end' of pain means its cessation or alleviation. The description of sattvic pleasure follows.

Knowledge, act and actor all serve the aim of happiness, which is threefold; in the best kind one gradually draws exquisite delight through long habituation and finally reaches the end of the pain of samsara.
Sattvic happiness is relished through familiarity, not suddenly like sense pleasure, and in it one reaches the cessation of all pain; it is like poison at first and nectar at the end (37).
Even a little of the pleasure experienced in the Self brings pain to an end; he cross-refers to 6.20-30 on the joy of meditation.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to encourage persistence: meditation, study, music, exercise or service may feel effortful at first, but the joy they give deepens with practice and outlasts quick pleasures.
misreadings: Not a promise that practice will remove all pain quickly.
Not dismissing ordinary pleasures; it contrasts depth and durability.
cautions: Gentle; 'end of sorrow' should not be framed as a deadline for someone grieving.
speaks_to: Starting a new practice and finding it hard
Seeking lasting rather than quick satisfaction
Habit-building and discipline
not_for: Fresh grief if framed as 'practice will end your sorrow'

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.39 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda)
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Last of three kinds of happiness (18.36-39). Sattvic happiness is bitter at first and nectar later; rajasic is sweet at first and poison later; this tamasic kind deludes from start to finish and comes from sleep, sloth and heedlessness. Krishna then says nothing in creation is free of the three gunas (18.40).

key_terms.sense: both at the start and in the aftermath
deluding, clouding the self
sleep, sloth and heedlessness

core_teaching: The lowest kind of happiness, born of dullness, laziness and inattention, clouds the mind both while it is enjoyed and afterwards.

commentaries.gist: Very brief: the pleasure that deludes the self both at first and 'in the sequel', meaning after it ends, and that arises from sleep, indolence and heedlessness, is tamasic.

It enthrals the self while enjoyed and when its results appear. Delusion hides things' true nature: sleep plainly does, sloth dulls the senses and so the intellect, heedlessness is inattention to the work at hand. So suppress rajas and tamas.
Self-deluding from the first moment and afterwards, it arises from sleep, lassitude and inadvertence, which he explains as fantasising while neglecting the duty at hand.
Gives the example of pleasure from habits like drinking liquor and eating worthless food, which makes one forget the path one should tread.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it to numbing pleasures: binge-watching, oversleeping, intoxication, idle fantasy. They feel like relief but leave you foggier.
misreadings: Not condemning rest, sleep or leisure in healthy measure.
Not a judgement on people with fatigue or illness.
cautions: Overlaps with exhaustion and depression; avoid shaming rest. Sivananda's mention of liquor needs care with readers in recovery.
speaks_to: Numbing habits and their aftermath
Wanting more nourishing leisure
Weekend lethargy and regret
not_for: Depression, chronic fatigue or illness
New parents and carers short of sleep

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.45 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda)
translation_note: Faithful. 'Perfection' (saṃsiddhi) is read by Shankara and Sridhara as fitness for knowledge, by Ramanuja as the final state; our 'fulfilment' in the line is a soft but acceptable rendering.
context: Krishna has just listed the duties that arise from the nature (svabhāva) of each of the four varṇas (18.41-44). Here he states the principle behind the list and announces that he will explain how one's own work leads to perfection; the next verse gives the answer: by worshipping, through that work, the one from whom all beings come.

key_terms.sense: wholeheartedly engaged, each in his own work
perfection, fulfilment; for Shankara the mind's fitness for knowledge
one's own duty, the work belonging to one's nature and station

core_teaching: Doing one's own work wholeheartedly is itself a path to the highest good; the commentators add that this works because such work, done without craving for results and as worship, purifies the mind for knowledge or devotion.

commentaries.gist: Each devoted to the duty ordained by his nature gains a perfection that is the body and senses made fit for the path of knowledge once their impurities are washed out; he notes duty alone does not directly give liberation.
Every person devoted to his own duty reaches the final state of perfection, the supreme abode; the following verses explain the manner.
Perfection here means fitness for knowledge; the verse and a half that follows explains how sincere performance of one's own duty leads to knowledge of the truth.

Do the duty that fits your nature wholeheartedly, without craving results, as an offering to God; this washes the mind's impurities and prepares it for self-knowledge, though works alone do not liberate.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to dignify ordinary work: putting full attention and integrity into the job in front of you, as an offering rather than a scramble for reward, is itself spiritual practice.
misreadings: Not a promise that any job brings success or status; 'perfection' is inner readiness, not worldly achievement.
Not a licence for workaholism; the stress is on the spirit of the work, not its quantity.
Not to be read as divine endorsement of caste-assigned occupations (see cautions).
cautions: The verse sits inside the varṇa list (18.41-48) and every classical commentator, and Sivananda, ties 'one's own work' to caste duty. Our misuse note ('the work that fits your nature', not birth) is a modern reading; present it as such rather than as what the commentaries say.
For someone unemployed or stuck in work they hate, 'perfection through your own work' can sound like blame.
speaks_to: Feeling your ordinary job is spiritually meaningless
Comparing your path with others' and feeling behind
Wanting to bring care and integrity to daily work
Early career: finding work that fits your temperament
not_for: Someone who has just lost their job
A person trapped in exploitative or abusive work
Readers sensitive to caste, if the context is not explained
research_note: Classical commentaries tie svakarma to varṇa duty; the 'work that fits your nature' reading in our misuse field is a modern interpretation and should be framed as such.

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.49 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda)
translation_note: Accurate. 'Renunciation' (saṃnyāsa) is read differently: Shankara takes it as right knowledge or formal renunciation of all action; Ramanuja and Sridhara as giving up attachment and fruit while still working.
context: After saying that one reaches perfection through one's own work offered to the Lord (18.45-48), Krishna turns to the higher perfection beyond that: the state of freedom from action. This verse names who reaches it, and the following verses (18.50-55) describe how such a person settles into Brahman.

key_terms.sense: mind unattached in every direction (Shankara: to children, spouse and possessions)
one who has mastered the mind
craving gone, for body, life and pleasures
the perfection of actionlessness; freedom from the bondage of action

core_teaching: When attachment, self-will and craving fall away, a person reaches a freedom in which action no longer binds; the schools differ on whether this means formal renunciation (Shankara) or a contemplative stillness reached while still doing one's duty (Ramanuja, Sridhara).

commentaries.gist: One whose mind clings to nothing, not even children or spouse, whose mind is controlled and who no longer craves body, life or pleasure, attains through knowledge-based renunciation the supreme actionlessness, immediate liberation, knowing the self as actionless Brahman.

Unattached to fruits, mind conquered, desire gone because all sense of being the doer is handed over to the Lord; through relinquishing fruits while still doing one's duty he reaches the highest stage of meditation, where the senses fall still.
Unattachment means no egotism and no desire for results; by renouncing attachment to work and its fruit he reaches a purity in which activity ceases, the state of the highest renunciate.
Free of attachment to family, body and property, the mind turns inward; knowing the Self, one may still act for the world's good yet is not bound, since the sense of being the doer has gone.

practical_reading: Modern teachers read it as inner freedom: you can keep working and caring while loosening the grip of needing outcomes, possessions and approval.
misreadings: Not a call to abandon family or responsibilities; Ramanuja and Sridhara keep the person working.
'Unattached' does not mean cold or indifferent to people.
Not a quick technique; the commentators place it at the end of a long discipline.
cautions: Shankara explicitly names detachment from children and spouse; in a reading for someone grieving or estranged from family this could sound like approval of withdrawal.
speaks_to: Exhaustion from needing every outcome to go your way
Wanting freedom from compulsive striving
Midlife questions about what you actually need
not_for: Someone isolated or estranged who may hear it as 'detach from people'
Fresh grief over a family member

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.53 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda)
translation_note: Accurate. 'Force' (bala) is specified by Shankara and Sivananda as strength fused with passion, not physical strength; Ramanuja reads it as the momentum of old habits. 'Possessiveness' (parigraha) is literally 'accumulated possessions'.
context: Krishna is describing the person who has reached the perfection of knowledge: pure in mind, steady, living simply in solitude (18.51-52). This verse lists what that person has dropped, and the next verse says that, having become Brahman, they neither grieve nor crave.

key_terms.sense: ego; identifying the self with the body
force; strength driven by passion (Shankara), or the pull of old habits (Ramanuja)
arrogance that leads one to overstep right conduct
possessions, the habit of acquiring and holding
without 'mine', at peace

core_teaching: Peace and fitness for the highest come from dropping a specific set of inner habits: ego, aggressive will, arrogance, craving, anger, accumulation, and the sense of ownership.

commentaries.gist: Ego is identifying with the body; strength means force fused with passion, not physical strength; arrogance follows elation and breaks dharma. He gives up even possessions needed for the body, becoming a wandering renunciate, fit for Brahman.

Ego is taking the not-self for the self; 'strength' is the force of old impressions feeding it; pride follows. Free of 'mine' and serene in the self's bliss, the meditator becomes fit to realise the self's true nature.
Even the ego of 'I am detached' is dropped, along with rashness, spiritual pride, desire and anger; free of 'mine' even toward what comes unasked, and tranquil, he can rest in 'I am Brahman'.
Notes that people grow arrogant through wealth or learning and then transgress; the aspirant regards even the body as not his own and so becomes peaceful and fit for Brahman.

practical_reading: Teachers turn the list into a self-audit: notice where you push, show off, accumulate, or say 'mine', and loosen one of these today; peace follows the loosening.
misreadings: Not a rule that owning things is sinful for householders; Shankara's 'even bodily necessities' applies to the formal renunciate.
Not telling anyone to suppress anger by force; the commentators speak of a mind that has outgrown it.
'Ego' here is not healthy self-respect or boundaries.
cautions: A long list of faults can feel like an indictment to someone already self-critical; offer one item, not all six.
speaks_to: Ambition that has turned into constant pushing
Arguments driven by needing to win
Clutter and the urge to acquire
Wanting a calmer, simpler life
not_for: Someone with low self-worth who needs encouragement, not a list of faults
A person being exploited who needs to assert themselves

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.54 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda)
translation_note: Accurate. Shankara records a variant reading meaning 'neither grieves nor exults'.
context: Continuing the portrait of the one fit to become Brahman (18.53), Krishna describes the result: serenity, no grief, no craving, equal regard for all beings, and supreme devotion. The next verse says that through this devotion one knows him truly and enters him.

key_terms.sense: having become Brahman; for Ramanuja, having realised the self's own pure nature
serene, clear in mind
neither grieves nor longs
the same toward all beings
supreme devotion to me

core_teaching: Inner clarity shows itself as freedom from both grief and craving and as equal regard for all, and this state opens into the highest devotion; Advaita reads that devotion as knowledge, Vishishtadvaita as loving bliss in God.

commentaries.gist: Having reached Brahman, serene, he does not grieve over failures or wants and longs for nothing; this describes his nature, not a command. He feels others' joys and pains as his own and attains the highest devotion, that of knowledge.

Becoming Brahman means realising the self as pure consciousness belonging to the Lord; unclouded, he grieves and longs for nothing besides God, is indifferent to all else, and gains supreme devotion, a rapturous joy in the Lord.

Resting in Brahman, he does not grieve for what is lost or crave what he lacks, since he no longer identifies with the body; free of likes and dislikes, he attains devotion that sees all beings as the Lord.
Adds that 'the same to all beings' can mean feeling others' pain as one's own: such a heart is tender, rejoices and suffers with others, and has dropped jealousy and prejudice.

practical_reading: Teachers present it as a picture of where practice leads, not a demand: a steadier heart that feels for everyone and is less tossed between loss and wanting.
misreadings: Not a command not to grieve; Shankara says it describes the nature of one established in Brahman.
'Same to all' is not emotional flatness; Shankara and Sivananda read it as feeling everyone's joy and pain as your own.
cautions: 'Neither grieves' will land badly on someone newly bereaved unless framed as a distant horizon rather than a standard to meet.
Ramanuja's 'indifference toward every creature except the Lord' is a strong phrasing that can sound cold; don't quote it to a lonely reader.
speaks_to: Longing for inner steadiness after a turbulent period
Swinging between disappointment and wanting more
Wanting to love people more evenly, beyond one's own circle
not_for: Fresh grief
Someone being told by others to 'just get over it'

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.56 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda)
translation_note: Accurate. 'Home' for padam is a warm rendering of 'state/abode'.
context: Having described the path of knowledge and renunciation (18.49-55), Krishna returns to the person who keeps working. This verse says that even one constantly busy with every kind of work reaches the eternal state by his grace if they rely on him; the next verse urges Arjuna to offer all action inwardly.

key_terms.sense: even while always doing all kinds of work
taking refuge in me; relying wholly on me
through my grace
the eternal, undecaying state or abode

core_teaching: A full, busy working life is no barrier to the highest goal, provided one relies on the divine rather than on one's own sense of being the doer; the result is a gift of grace, not a wage.

commentaries.gist: Whoever does all actions, even forbidden ones, yet takes refuge in the Lord with the whole self centred in him reaches by the Lord's grace the eternal abode of Vishnu.
All works, including those done with a desire, performed while ascribing all authorship to the Lord and trusting him, lead to him, the goal that is eternal and infinite.

Concludes how worship through one's duties brings liberation: doing regular, occasional and even desire-prompted acts in the way described, with the Lord as sole refuge instead of heaven as the aim, one reaches his eternal state by grace.
Worship the Lord with the flowers of good actions; work done as worship purifies the heart. Like drains flowing into the Ganga, the devotee merged in the Lord is not tainted by occasional lapses.

practical_reading: Teachers use it for busy people: you don't have to leave your job or family to grow spiritually; keep the work, change what you lean on.
misreadings: Not 'anything goes if you are devoted'; Shankara's and Sivananda's mention of forbidden acts concerns grace toward lapses, not permission.
Not a promise of worldly success; the 'home' is the spiritual goal.
Not saying effort is pointless because grace does it all; the person keeps working.
cautions: The classical gloss that even prohibited actions do not bar the devotee can be misused to excuse harm; leave it out of readings.
speaks_to: Busy professionals or parents who feel too occupied for spiritual life
Guilt about not having time to practise
Burnout from carrying everything alone
not_for: Someone rationalising harmful behaviour
A person told their suffering is 'grace' and should not be challenged

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.57 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda)
translation_note: Accurate. 'Yoga of understanding' (buddhi-yoga) is glossed as steady-mindedness and firm faith (Shankara), as the yoga of wisdom in which God is seen as goal (Ramanuja), and as resolute intellect (Sridhara).
context: Following the promise that one who keeps working while relying on the Lord reaches him (18.56), Krishna turns it into direct instruction to Arjuna: offer all action inwardly, keep him as the goal and the mind on him. The next verse states the result and the danger of ego.

key_terms.sense: inwardly laying down, handing over, all actions to me
holding me as the highest goal
the discipline of steady, discerning understanding
mind always on me

core_teaching: Surrender here is inner, not outer: keep acting, but hand over the sense of ownership and authorship, hold the divine as the goal, and keep the mind steady on it.

commentaries.gist: With the discerning faith that knowledge, not works, finally liberates, dedicate all actions with visible and invisible results to the Lord as in 9.27, regard him as the goal and rest on steady-mindedness as your refuge.
Dedicate in thought, knowing your self belongs to and is guided by the Lord, both the doership and the object of your works to him; doing everything with him as goal and fruit is buddhi-yoga.
Offer all actions to the Lord mentally, treat him as life's highest end, and, even while working, keep the mind fixed on him through a resolute intellect, as in 4.24's 'the offering is Brahman'.
Surrender all actions to the Lord while holding to discrimination; through it you see yourself as distinct from body and activity and resting in his being.

practical_reading: Teachers make it a daily practice: before a task, offer it inwardly; during it, keep returning attention to what you serve; after it, let go of the result.
misreadings: Not quitting one's work; the giving-up is mental (cetasā).
Not abandoning judgement; buddhi-yoga means more discernment, not less.
speaks_to: Anxiety about outcomes at work
Feeling scattered and needing one anchor
Wanting to turn routine work into practice
not_for: Someone who reads 'surrender' as passivity in a situation that needs action

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.58 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda). Govindacharya splits the verse: its first half is printed as 57a and the comment on 'if from egotism' as 58.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Obstacles' (durgāṇi) is literally 'hard places, fortresses'; Shankara takes them as the obstacles of saṃsāra born of ignorance.
context: Right after telling Arjuna to keep his mind on him (18.57), Krishna states the two outcomes: with mind on him, grace carries him through every difficulty; refusing out of ego leads to ruin. The next verses warn that Arjuna's own nature will make him fight anyway.

key_terms.sense: all difficult passes, obstacles
by my grace you will cross over
out of ego; Shankara and Sridhara: thinking oneself wise
you will perish, be ruined

core_teaching: Turned toward the divine, a person is carried through difficulties by grace; the real danger is the ego that thinks it already knows better and will not listen.

commentaries.gist: With your heart on the Lord, by his grace you cross the hard obstacles rooted in ignorance; if you refuse out of the conceit of being learned, or think 'I am independent, why obey another', you will be ruined.
Ego is the notion 'I know well what should and should not be done'; ignoring the Lord on that basis brings ruin, since no creature but he truly knows what is right or governs as he does.
Fixing your mind on him, you overcome all worldly troubles by grace; if from the notion that you are wise you will not listen, you fail to reach life's goal.

Through one-pointed devotion you cross pitfalls, temptations, illness and the other troubles of saṃsāra; but if through pride you disregard the teaching, thinking 'I know everything', you will be ruined.

practical_reading: Teachers read it as a warning about the know-it-all mind: when stuck, the block is often the refusal to listen; humility opens a way through.
misreadings: Not a threat of divine punishment for doubt; the commentators locate the ruin in acting from conceit.
Not a demand to obey any human authority who claims to speak for God.
cautions: 'You will perish' is harsh language; for an anxious or scrupulous reader, frame it as a natural consequence of ego, not a threat.
Can be weaponised by controlling teachers or relatives demanding obedience.
speaks_to: Facing a hard stretch and needing reassurance
Stubbornness that is costing you
Pride that blocks you from asking for help
not_for: Anxious or scrupulous readers prone to fear of punishment
Someone in a coercive religious or family setting

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.62 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda)
translation_note: Accurate. 'Him' refers to the Lord dwelling in the hearts of all beings (18.61).
context: Krishna has just said that the Lord dwells in the heart of every being and turns them as if mounted on a machine by his power (18.61). Here he tells Arjuna to take refuge in that Lord with his whole being. Next he says he has now taught the most secret wisdom and leaves Arjuna to reflect and choose (18.63).

key_terms.sense: go to him alone for refuge
with your whole being, in every way
supreme peace
the eternal abode or state

core_teaching: Complete, wholehearted refuge in the Lord within brings peace and the lasting goal as his gift; Ramanuja adds that refuge means following his guidance in what one actually does.

commentaries.gist: Seek the Lord as sole refuge with your whole being for relief from the distress of saṃsāra; by his grace you will gain supreme peace and the supreme eternal abode.

Take refuge in the governor of all who, out of love, became your charioteer: follow his directions, including fighting the war; obedience brings, by grace, peace as the end of karmic bonds and the eternal state.
Since every soul depends on the Lord, give up self-conceit and take refuge in him with all your heart; by his grace you gain supreme peace and his eternal abode.
Surrender totally and keep no secret desires; desire and ego are the two main obstacles to surrender; run to the Lord for shelter from the sorrows of saṃsāra.

practical_reading: Teachers read refuge as trust lived out: bring your whole self, worries included, to the divine, and act from that trust rather than from fear.
misreadings: Not giving up effort or judgement; the very next verse asks Arjuna to reflect fully and then choose.
Not refuge in a human guru or institution.
cautions: Ramanuja's reading that refuge means carrying out God's directions, including the war, should not become 'do what you are told'.
speaks_to: Feeling overwhelmed and needing to lean on something larger
Anxiety that comes from trying to control everything
A crisis where one has done what one can
not_for: Someone being told to 'just surrender' instead of getting medical or practical help
A reader without theistic belief, unless reframed

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.64 (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda). Sridhara notes a variant reading 'dṛḍhamati' (of firm resolve) for 'dṛḍham iti'.
translation_note: Accurate. 'Deeply loved' renders iṣṭo 'si me dṛḍham; Shankara glosses it as 'my firm friend, ever beloved'.
context: Krishna has just left Arjuna free to reflect and choose (18.63). Now, unprompted, he says he will repeat the most secret teaching once more because Arjuna is dear to him. The next two verses (18.65-66) give that teaching: fix your mind on me and take refuge in me alone.

key_terms.sense: most secret of all
the highest word
you are firmly dear to me
what is truly good for you

core_teaching: The final teaching is given out of love rather than duty or gain: the teacher repeats what matters most because the student is dear.

commentaries.gist: Though already said more than once, the Lord repeats it not from fear or hope of reward but because Arjuna is his firm, beloved friend; what he will tell is the highest good, the means to knowledge.
Of the three paths, bhakti-yoga is pre-eminent and so most secret (as in 9.1); because Arjuna is dear and devoted, the Lord again states what is for his good.
For those unable to absorb the whole profound teaching, the Lord kindly gives its essence in three verses; he repeats it because Arjuna is very dear to him.
The repetition is to make a deep impression; Krishna seeks nothing from Arjuna, who is his beloved friend and disciple, and so tells him the supreme good.

practical_reading: Teachers stress the tenderness: before the hardest truth, Krishna reassures Arjuna that he is loved; good counsel lands best when the listener knows they are cared for.
misreadings: Not favouritism toward a chosen few; the commentators tie it to Arjuna's devotion and readiness.
speaks_to: Feeling unloved or unworthy
Needing to hear something important from someone who cares
Mentors and parents wanting to give counsel with warmth
not_for: Little risk; may feel hollow to someone grieving the loss of the person who loved them most

verified_ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.78, the final verse (same number in Mahadeva Sastri's Shankara, Govindacharya's Ramanuja, Vireswarananda's Sridhara and Sivananda)
translation_note: Translation accurate. Our 'line' ('where wisdom and skilled effort stand together') is a modern allegorical gloss, not what the verse or commentators say; nīti is 'policy/statesmanship/right conduct', so 'steady justice' is loose.
context: Krishna has asked whether Arjuna's delusion is gone; Arjuna says it is and that he will do as told (18.72-73). Sanjaya, who has narrated the whole dialogue to the blind king Dhritarashtra, describes his thrill at hearing it and closes with this conviction about which side will prevail.

key_terms.sense: Krishna, lord of yoga, source of all yoga
Arjuna, the bow-bearer (with the Gandiva bow)
fortune, victory, flourishing prosperity
sure, firm statecraft or right conduct

core_teaching: Where the divine guide and the committed doer stand together, success and right order follow; for Sanjaya this is also a pointed hint to the king about the war's outcome.

commentaries.gist: Glosses briefly: 'wherever' means on whichever side; Krishna is lord of yoga since all yoga springs from him; the archer bears the Gandiva; 'there' is the Pandavas' side, where fortune, victory, growing prosperity and policy stand.
Krishna is lord of every arrangement of beings, governing all; where he and Partha, whose only refuge is the Lord's feet, are together, fortune, victory, power and righteousness dwell permanently.

Sanjaya is hinting to Dhritarashtra to give up hope for his sons' rule, seek Krishna's refuge and make peace with the Pandavas; he then sums up the Gita as devotion, aided by self-knowledge given by grace, leading to liberation.
Calls this the 'one-verse Gita', whose recitation carries the merit of the whole; follows Shankara's gloss on 'wherever' and 'lord of yoga'.

practical_reading: Teachers apply it as a partnership: inner guidance and wholehearted effort together; neither prayer without action nor action without guidance.
misreadings: Not a guarantee of worldly success to anyone who claims God is on their side.
The 'wisdom plus effort' reading is a modern allegory; the commentators read it literally about Krishna, Arjuna and the war.
cautions: Victory language can sound triumphal to someone who has just failed or lost; avoid pairing with defeat.
speaks_to: Starting a venture and wanting to align effort with guidance
Teams: the value of a guide and a doer working together
Closing a period of study or reflection
not_for: Someone who has just failed and may hear it as 'you lacked God'
Partisan or 'God is on our side' contexts
research_note: Our 'line' gives a modern allegorical reading; label it as such or bring it closer to the text.
